_README: Rich topics. The input to the Editorial Reel, and the replacement for the
hook+punchline pairs in topics.json.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
A topic in topics.json is about ten words. A thirty-second video needs
roughly eighty. generate-shorts.mjs closed that gap with filler, and in one
case with a number drawn at random from a pool and captioned 'Mind the
number.' A video about Nintendo's founding showed '5'. That is the failure
this file exists to make impossible: a topic either carries real content or
it does not get made into a video.
THE verified FLAG IS LOAD-BEARING
generate-reels.mjs refuses to emit props for a topic with verified:false
unless --allow-unverified is passed, and that flag also stamps the props so
the render is obviously a draft. Nothing unverified can reach a channel by
accident. Set verified:true only when every factual claim in the beats is
backed by an entry in sources, and you have actually read them.
ON NUMBERS SPECIFICALLY
A figure beat renders a value at 300px. That is an enormous claim to make.
Only add one where the number is real, specific and sourced. Most topics
below have no figure beat, because forcing one would mean inventing it, and
a four-beat video is the correct answer to not having a fifth true thing to
say. Being true is not enough either: a number that only two credible
sources disagree about, or that is an address, a duration or a count that
happens to exist, does not deserve to be the biggest thing on screen. Every
topic here that has no figure beat says in its verifiedNote which number was
considered and why it was cut. Read that before adding one back.
AND KEEP unit SHORT — IT CANNOT WRAP
FigureBeat lays the value and the unit out in one flex row with no wrap and
no shrink: 300px value, 22px gap, 76px unit, inside PAD=72 either side. That
leaves roughly 550px of unit for a two-digit value, which is about nine
characters. 'photoreceptors' was rendered and ran off the right edge with the
final s missing; it is 'receptors' now. Nothing warns about this — the only
way it shows up is rendering the reel and looking at it, so do that.
AND value MUST BE A WHOLE NUMBER
FigureBeat animates a count-up, and it derives the target with
parseInt(String(value).replace(/[^0-9]/g, '')). Every non-digit is deleted,
not parsed. '37.1' becomes the target 371 and renders as a giant 371. '1,300'
becomes 1300, '2.1' becomes 21. There is no warning and the props are valid;
you get a confidently wrong number at 300px, which is the exact failure this
file exists to prevent. Put the whole number in value and the precision in
context — tardigrade-heat shows 37 and says 37.1 underneath.
NO AMBIENT BED. THIS IS DELIBERATE.
The beds in public/sounds/ are synthesised from filtered noise. They were
normalised to fix a real problem (renders measured -43dB, silent on a phone)
and that made the wrong thing louder: amplified broad-spectrum noise reads as
radio static, not atmosphere. Four Reels shipped sounding like a broken radio
before anyone listened, because the check was a loudness measurement and not
an ear. Loud is not the same as good.
Silence is better than hiss. A Reel is watched muted more often than not, and
a clean silent video beats a noisy one. Narration still plays where a topic
has it. Do not restore a bed until there is real recorded ambience to use.
BEAT KINDS available: code, statement, credit, figure, kicker, sign.
Durations are NOT set here. generate-reels.mjs computes them from how long
each beat takes to animate and read, or from voiceCuts when a narration
track has been measured.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuhisa_Hashimoto — Hashimoto (1958-2020) created the code while porting the arcade Gradius to the NES in 1986; he added a sequence granting full power-ups so he could finish the game for in-house testing, and intended to remove it before ship.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami_Code — the game shipped with the code still in it; players found it and reported it back to Konami. Wider fame came with Contra in 1988, where the code granted additional lives.
https://www.npr.org/2020/02/26/809622331/kazuhisa-hashimoto-creator-of-famous-konami-code-gaming-cheat-dies — obituary confirming authorship and the Gradius origin.

https://contra.fandom.com/wiki/Konami_Code — the Contra figure specifically: the code gives 30 lives, shown in-game as 'Rest 30'. Corroborated by multiple cheat references; the code is commonly called the 30 Lives Code.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. The '30 lives' figure was the one worth confirming separately from the origin story — Wikipedia says only 'additional lives', so the number comes from the Contra-specific sources. The beat text is left exactly as rendered because the narration track is cut to it; changing a word would desync voiceCuts.

beats.lead: But here is the part nobody says
beats.text: It was never meant to ship.
beats.note: The Konami Code was debug scaffolding. It was supposed to be deleted before release.

beats.name: Kazuhisa Hashimoto
beats.role: Porting Gradius to the NES. He could not get through his own game well enough to test it, so he wrote a shortcut that handed the player every power-up at once.

beats.context: What the same code granted in Contra, two years later. That is the version most people remember.

beats.text: He forgot to take it out.

beats.line: A bug that outlived the console.

sources: https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/object/nmah_334663 — the Smithsonian National Museum of American History's own catalogue entry for the log book with the moth still taped in.
https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/september/9/ — date and machine: 9 September 1947, Harvard Mark II.

https://daily.jstor.org/the-bug-in-the-computer-bug-story/ — the correction that matters: 'bug' for a technical fault predates 1947 by over a century, back to Edison, so this was never the coining of the term.

https://www.pricefx.com/learning-center/software-engineering-debacles-grace-hopper-and-the-first-reported-bug — the logbook wording: '15:45 Relay #70 Panel F (moth) in relay. First actual case of bug being found.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. Grace Hopper is deliberately NOT named. Sources agree she was on the Mark II team and popularised the story in later lectures, but the log book was probably not hers and the attribution is contested. The beats credit the machine and an unnamed operator instead, which is what the evidence actually supports. The joke in the note beat — that engineers had used 'bug' for decades before one turned out to be literal — is the JSTOR correction, used as the hook rather than buried. There WAS a figure beat here showing 70, the relay number, and it was cut. The number is true and sourced, but a figure beat renders its value at 300px, and the relay number carries no significance whatsoever — it is an address, not a fact. Setting it that large would have overstated it. Being true is not sufficient; a number given that much emphasis has to deserve it. The detail now sits in a statement beat where it reads as the log entry it actually is.

beats.lead: The word is older than the machine
beats.text: One day the bug was literal.
beats.note: Engineers had called faults bugs since Edison. On this one afternoon, someone opened a relay and found an actual insect.

beats.name: Harvard Mark II
beats.role: 9 September. An operator traced a fault to a moth caught in a relay, removed it, and taped it into the log book instead of throwing it away.

beats.lead: What they wrote in the log
beats.text: First actual case of bug being found.
beats.note: Relay #70, Panel F. 15:45. The wording gives it away — they knew the joke they were making.

beats.text: They kept the moth.

beats.line: It is still taped to the page, in the Smithsonian.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Tesler — joined Xerox PARC in 1973; worked with Tim Mott on the Gypsy text editor; developed cut, copy and paste and the principle of modeless software. Died 2020, aged 74.
https://worrydream.com/refs/Tesler_2012_-_A_Personal_History_of_Modeless_Text_Editing_and_Cut-Copy-Paste.pdf — Tesler's own 2012 account, the primary source for how the commands came about.
https://www.fastcompany.com/90466328/a-tribute-to-larry-tesler-the-father-of-user-friendly-design — the NO MODES number plate, and the framing of modelessness as his life's argument.
https://www.tiny.cloud/blog/copy-paste-inventor/ — Gypsy dated to 1974-75 and the mechanics of the modeless selection it introduced.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 11 Aug 2026. Tim Mott is credited alongside Tesler in every source, so the credit beat names both — 'invented by Larry Tesler' alone is the popular shorthand and it is not quite right. No figure beat: there is no real number here, and a usage statistic would have had to be invented, which is the exact thing this file exists to prevent. The NO MODES plate is real and does the work a number would have. The Businessweek beat was added after seeing the first render: at four beats this ran 19s, and because credit and kicker both paint the dark background, the middle sat on two identical frames back to back. The fix for a thin video is another true thing to say, not a longer hold — and the June 1975 feature is sourced. Note the wording is deliberately 'turned up in': the article was titled The Office of the Future and mentioned Gypsy, it was not a piece about Gypsy, and 'Businessweek wrote it up' would have overstated that.

beats.lead: You did it today without thinking
beats.text: Someone had to invent cut and paste.
beats.note: Before it existed, moving text meant retyping it — or literally cutting the paper and pasting it down. The names are not a metaphor.

beats.name: Tesler and Mott
beats.role: At Xerox PARC they built a text editor called Gypsy, where selecting text and moving it worked the same way every time, with no hidden mode to remember first.

beats.lead: It was news at the time
beats.text: In 1975 it turned up in Businessweek.
beats.note: In a feature called The Office of the Future. The idea was worth reporting before it was furniture.

beats.text: His number plate read NO MODES.

sources: https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/a-different-form-of-color-vision-in-mantis-shrimp/ — the institutional record of the paper, carrying the full Science abstract: Thoen, How, Chiou & Marshall, 'A different form of color vision in mantis shrimp', Science 343(6169):411-413, 24 Jan 2014, PMID 24458639. Establishes the 12 photoreceptor types sampling 300-720nm, that three or four are sufficient for fine colour discrimination, the 'surprisingly poor' behavioural wavelength discrimination, and the temporal-scanning recognition hypothesis.

https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/the-mantis-shrimp-sees-like-a-satellite — Ed Yong's report from the week of publication. Source for the discrimination numbers actually put on screen: humans separate wavelengths about 5nm apart, the shrimp only 15-25nm. Also the species tested (Haptosquilla trispinosa), the training method, and Justin Marshall's own framing — 'Actually, they're much worse!' and the satellite lookup-table comparison.
https://www.calacademy.org/explore-science/mantis-shrimp-vision — California Academy of Sciences, checked as a third institutional statement of the same finding.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 12 and it earns the 300px: the entire popular myth is built on that number, so the video's turn only works if the number is the biggest thing on screen first. Note that this batch also contains vanilla-albius, whose emotional core is a twelve-year-old — that topic was deliberately given NO figure beat rather than a second giant '12' on the same channel. Do not 'improve' it by adding one back. Deliberately not said: any claim about how many colours the animal sees. Sources agree on receptor count, not on any colour count, and '100,000 colours' style figures are invented. The 8-visible/4-UV split comes from Yong; the abstract only gives the 300-720nm range, so the split is stated as description rather than as the headline number. The unit reads 'receptors' and not 'photoreceptors' for a layout reason, not a factual one: the first render clipped 'photoreceptors' off the right edge of the frame, because FigureBeat puts the unit on one unwrapped line beside a 300px number. Do not lengthen it back. 'You manage five' is the human 5nm discrimination threshold from Yong, rounded as he gives it. The mechanism beat says 'may not compare colours at all' rather than asserting it — the paper itself says 'suggest', and Marshall's own quoted answer to what they do instead was 'Dunno'.

beats.text: It is not what you were told.
beats.note: The mantis shrimp is famous for seeing colours you cannot imagine. In 2014 someone tested what it can actually tell apart.

beats.context: Eight across the range you can see, four more in the ultraviolet. You have three. Four is already enough for fine colour discrimination.

beats.text: It is worse at this than you are.
beats.note: It could only separate wavelengths fifteen to twenty-five nanometres apart. You manage five. So do honeybees.

beats.name: Hanne Thoen
beats.role: Working in Justin Marshall's lab in Queensland, she found the eye may not compare colours at all. It scans, and matches the reading against something like a lookup table.

beats.text: It is not seeing more. It is seeing faster.

beats.line: The best-known fact about this animal is the wrong one.

sources: https://www.eso.org/public/news/eso2109/ — ESO's release on Montargès et al., Nature, 16 June 2021. Establishes the dimming through late 2019 and early 2020, the VLT images, and that the star was partially concealed by a cloud of dust.

https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/news/mystery-solved-dust-cloud-led-betelgeuses-great-dimming — Harvard & Smithsonian CfA, same date, independent institution. Source for 'lost more than two-thirds of its brightness', the January and March 2020 images, the mechanism (ejected gas bubble, a patch of surface cooled, heavier elements such as silicon condensed into dust), the return to normal brightness by April 2020, and Montargès' line about watching a star's appearance change in real time on a scale of weeks.

https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-finds-that-betelgeuses-mysterious-dimming-is-due-to-a-traumatic-outburst/ — Dupree's earlier Hubble work, reaching the dust conclusion by a different route and independently.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.05982 — the dissent, read and deliberately accounted for: 'The Photospheric Temperatures of Betelgeuse during the Great Dimming of 2019/2020: No New Dust Required'.
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-25018-3 — 'Spectroscopic evidence for a large spot on the dimming Betelgeuse', the competing large-cool-spot emphasis.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, on purpose. The candidates were the V-band magnitude at minimum (1.6, jargon that means nothing at 300px), the fraction of light lost (given variously as 'more than two-thirds', '70%' and '1.2 magnitudes' — approximate, and stated differently by each source), and 200,000 mph for the ejected material (single-sourced to Dupree). None of them is both crisp and load-bearing, so the topic runs on the correction instead. The dust explanation is stated as the answer astronomers arrived at, which is what ESO, CfA and NASA all say — but the exact mechanism is genuinely still argued, with at least one paper titled 'No New Dust Required' and another pushing a large cool spot. The beat wording follows CfA's version (gas ejected, surface patch cools, silicon condenses) because that account is compatible with the cool-spot camp rather than opposed to it. Do not upgrade 'the answer came' to 'proven'. Also deliberately not said: the distance to Betelgeuse, and any timescale for the supernova. Both are quoted with enormous error bars and neither survives being set in type.

beats.lead: Late in 2019 a star started going out
beats.text: The headlines said supernova.
beats.note: Betelgeuse, the orange shoulder of Orion, lost more than two thirds of its light by February 2020. Then it came back.

beats.name: Betelgeuse
beats.role: A red supergiant close enough that a telescope can resolve its actual surface. Between January and March, astronomers watched the southern half of it darken, week by week.

beats.text: It was dust.
beats.note: The star threw off a bubble of gas. A patch of surface behind it cooled, silicon condensed, and it hid behind its own soot.

beats.text: It will explode. That was not it.

beats.line: Still there. Still the shoulder of Orion.

sources: https://www.linnean.org/news/2019/10/16/edmond-albius — the Linnean Society's account, which quotes Ferréol Bellier-Beaumont's own 1861 letter to the Justice of the Peace at Sainte-Suzanne ('I taught the little black boy, Edmond, how to marry the male and female parts together... This clever boy had realized that the vanilla flower also had male and female elements'), his rebuttal of Jean Michel Claude Richard's counter-claim ('How could Mr. Richard have taught the young boy this technique in 1838 — when he was only eight years old?'), the 20-year-old barren vine, the 1880 Moniteur death notice, and Arditti et al. 2009's conclusion that the discovery was Albius's own.

https://www.europeana.eu/en/stories/edmond-albius — Europeana, story contributed by the Fondation pour la Mémoire de l'Esclavage. Independently gives birth at Sainte-Suzanne on 9 August 1829, the 1841 discovery at twelve, freedom in 1848, death in poverty in 1880, and that the hand-pollination method is still used worldwide.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Albius — checked only to confirm the age at discovery agrees with the two above.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and the reason is editorial rather than factual: his age is well sourced and would have made a strong 300px '12', but mantis-shrimp-colour in this same batch already puts a giant 12 on the same channel, and two videos opening on the same numeral would read as a template. The age is carried in the credit beat instead. If mantis-shrimp-colour is ever retired, this is the topic that should get the figure beat back. Deliberately left out: all tonnage figures. The Linnean Society gives Réunion exports as 2 tonnes in 1858, 20 in 1867, 200 in 1898; Europeana gives about 1 tonne a year in the 1850s, 15 in the following decade, 60 by the early 1880s. Those do not reconcile, so no export number appears anywhere. Also left out: what crop gave him the idea. Bellier-Beaumont's own letter says watermelon, Europeana says pumpkin, and rather than pick one the beat now just says he worked it out himself. Deliberately included, because it is the actual correction: Albius was not the first to hand-pollinate vanilla — Charles Morren published the technique in 1837, four years earlier — but Morren's method suited a greenhouse and not a plantation. The beats therefore never say he was first, only that the method that scaled was his. Do not add 'invented'.

beats.lead: Almost every vanilla pod you have eaten
beats.text: Was pollinated by hand.
beats.note: The orchid has its own bee only in Mexico. Everywhere else someone opens each flower and does it themselves, one at a time.

beats.name: Edmond Albius
beats.role: Twelve, born into slavery on Réunion and taught horticulture by the man who owned him. He saw the flower's two halves were separated by a flap you could lift.

beats.lead: His owner did not believe it
beats.text: Then more pods appeared.
beats.note: Bellier-Beaumont had kept one barren vine alive twenty years. In 1861 he wrote that the boy worked it out himself.

beats.text: He said he taught the boy.
beats.note: Bellier-Beaumont checked the dates: by that account Edmond was eight. Archivists went back over it in 2009 and agreed it was his.

beats.text: He died in a public hospital with nothing.

beats.line: The method has not changed since.

sources: https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/1816-the-year-without-summer.htm — US National Park Service. Source for the Tambora attribution, the nicknames ('Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death'), and every weather detail on screen: May frost killing crops in New York, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont; June snow at Albany, New York and Dennysville, Maine; lakes and rivers still frozen in July as far south as north-western Pennsylvania.

https://www.gutenberg.org/files/42324/42324-h/42324-h.htm — Project Gutenberg's text of the 1831 Frankenstein, where Mary Shelley's own author's introduction gives the quoted words: 'it proved a wet, ungenial summer, and incessant rain often confined us for days to the house.'
https://www.britannica.com/event/Haunted-Summer-of-1816 — Britannica on the Villa Diodati party (Byron, Percy and Mary, Claire Clairmont, Polidori) and the ghost-story agreement.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer — checked for the global temperature anomaly, which is why no temperature figure appears here.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and no temperature anywhere. The NPS says the cloud 'changed the global climate by 2-7 degrees Fahrenheit'; Wikipedia gives the global average anomaly as 0.4-0.7°C, which is about 0.7-1.3°F. Those are different claims — one is almost certainly regional and the other a global mean — and putting either at 300px would be asserting a precision the sources do not share. The causal chain is deliberately only half-drawn. Tambora causing the cold is stated, because NPS states it directly. Tambora causing Frankenstein is NOT stated: the beats put the party indoors in the rain and quote Mary Shelley's own account of why, and stop there. 'A volcano wrote Frankenstein' was drafted as the kicker and cut, because it is the sort of tidy line that is repeated until it becomes a fact. The kicker used instead — that nobody in the room knew why it was raining — is the true and better point. Also note 1816 was already sitting on a cold decade and there was an earlier unidentified eruption around 1808-09, so Tambora is the trigger rather than the whole explanation; the credit beat says it 'put enough into the stratosphere to shade the planet', which is what the source supports, and not 'caused'.

beats.lead: In 1816 the summer did not arrive
beats.text: It snowed in June.
beats.note: May frost killed the crops across New England. June snow fell on Albany. In July there was still ice on Pennsylvania rivers.

beats.name: Mount Tambora
beats.role: An Indonesian volcano had erupted the year before and put enough into the stratosphere to shade the planet. Nobody in New England made the connection.

beats.text: It rained for days.
beats.note: Byron, the Shelleys and Polidori were shut inside a rented villa. To fill the evenings they each agreed to write a ghost story.

beats.text: A wet, ungenial summer.
beats.note: Her words: incessant rain often confined us for days to the house. She was eighteen. What she started that week was Frankenstein.

beats.text: Nobody in that room knew why.

beats.line: They called it eighteen hundred and froze to death.

sources: https://core.tdar.org/project/459204/atari-dump-site-alamogordo-new-mexico-usa — the Digital Archaeological Record's project entry, the primary archaeological record (project director Andrew Reinhard, field director Richard Rothaus, PI Joe Lewandowski; doi:10.48512/XCV8459204). Establishes the September 1983 deposit, that it was reported at the time in the New York Times and the Alamogordo Daily News before becoming an urban legend, the 26 April 2014 excavation by the City of Alamogordo with archaeologists and a film crew, 'recovered just over 1,300 games', the 10-metre depth, the manifest as the most important result, and the receiving institutions: the Smithsonian, the Tularosa Basin Historical Museum, The Strong National Museum of Play, the Henry Ford, and VIGAMUS in Rome.

https://www.thehenryford.org/collections/explore/artifact/403653 — the Henry Ford's own catalogue entry for an excavated E.T. cartridge (object ID 2015.13.15, gift of the City of Alamogordo), independently confirming the 26 April 2014 date and that the material is now museum-accessioned.
https://archaeology.org/issues/july-august-2014/digs-discoveries/new-mexico-atari-dump-site-excavation/ — Archaeology Magazine's contemporaneous write-up of the dig.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and the count of buried cartridges is deliberately absent from every beat. tDAR says 'ca. 800,000'; the Henry Ford says 700,000. Both are credible primary-adjacent institutions and they do not agree, so the beats say 'hundreds of thousands' and nothing more precise. The recovered count is given as 'just over 1,300' — tDAR's own wording — rather than the 1,382 that circulates in press coverage, because tDAR is the excavation's own record and the press figure could not be traced to it. A figure beat was drafted twice and cut twice: first with the buried count (contested, see above), then with 31, the years between burial and dig. 31 is true and arithmetic from two solid dates, but it is a duration, and a duration at 300px implies a significance it does not have. The story is the myth turning out to be documented, not any one number. Also not said: that concrete was poured over the cell. It is repeated everywhere and appears in none of the three sources read here.

beats.lead: For thirty years this was a rumour
beats.text: Atari buried its games in the desert.
beats.note: September 1983: trucks took hundreds of thousands of cartridges out to a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico, and buried them.

beats.name: Alamogordo, New Mexico
beats.role: The New York Times reported it at the time. Then it slid out of the record and became a story gamers told each other, always about E.T.

beats.text: All of it was true.
beats.note: The city, archaeologists and a film crew went ten metres down and pulled up just over 1,300 cartridges. Not only E.T.

beats.text: The Smithsonian took some.
beats.note: So did the Henry Ford, the Strong Museum of Play and the video game museum in Rome. A landfill became a catalogued site.

beats.text: The urban legend had a manifest.

sources: http://kanji.zinbun.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~yasuoka/publications/PreQWERTY.html — Koichi Yasuoka and Motoko Yasuoka, 'On the Prehistory of QWERTY', ZINBUN No.42 (March 2011), pp.161-174, with the authors' own abstract. The 'to slow down the operator' answer is quoted there and called, in their word, nonsense. Also the derivation from the Hughes-Phelps printing telegraph, the development for Morse receivers, and that the arrangement changed repeatedly and 'accidentally grew into QWERTY'.

https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/the-qwerty-keyboard-will-never-die-where-did-the-150-year-old-design-come-from-49863249/ — Smithsonian Magazine, quoting the paper directly for the Morse detail used on screen: American Morse renders Z as '... .', easily confused with the digram SE, so S needed to sit near both Z and E. Also Sholes' 1868 typewriter patent, and his 1889 application for an XPMCH layout filed a year before his death.

https://oztypewriter.blogspot.com/2012/10/on-this-day-in-typewriter-history-from.html — independent confirmation of the two dates put on screen: Sholes applied for design 568,630 in September 1889 and died at Milwaukee on 17 February 1890, the patent being assigned after his death.
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Christopher-Latham-Sholes — checked for Sholes' dates (1819-1890).
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat: the available numbers are the 1874 price of $125, and Remington's 1891 claim of 100,000 machines in use. Both are true and both are beside the point, which is that the reason everyone gives for the layout is wrong. The Morse Z/SE claim is the Yasuokas' argument, not an independently established fact, and the beat is worded to attribute it — 'their evidence' — rather than to state it as settled. It is worth knowing that the jamming account is not universally abandoned; Smithsonian describes it as contentious rather than dead, so the beats say the researchers who traced the history called it nonsense, which is precisely what happened, instead of saying it has been disproved. The code beat carries QWERTYUIOP rather than QWERTY because the ten-glyph top row is what a viewer recognises on sight and it gives the CodeBeat stagger enough to work with. The kicker is the real find: the man who gave us the layout filed a patent for a different one in September 1889 and was dead by the following February, so he spent his last months trying to replace it.

beats.caption: You have never once questioned this.

beats.text: It was built to slow you down.
beats.note: So the typebars would not jam. It is in textbooks. The researchers who traced the layout's real history called that, in print, nonsense.

beats.name: Koichi and Motoko Yasuoka
beats.role: At Kyoto University they followed the keyboard back past the typewriter to the telegraph. Its first heavy users were Morse operators taking down code live.

beats.text: American Morse writes Z almost like S-E.
beats.note: An operator could not tell them apart until the following letters arrived. So S ended up next to both Z and E.

beats.text: Sholes spent his last year trying to replace it.

beats.line: You are typing on his rough draft.

sources: https://doi.org/10.1091/mbc.E16-07-0509 — Michael W. Gray, 'Lynn Margulis and the endosymbiont hypothesis: 50 years later', Molecular Biology of the Cell 28(10), 2017 (PMC5426843, PMID 28495966), full text retrieved via PubMed. Establishes the three organelles she claimed (mitochondria, plastids, and the (9+2) basal bodies of flagella), that mitochondria trace to the α-Proteobacteria and plastids to the Cyanobacteria and that we know this 'through the genomes contained in' them, and — critically — that for the flagellum claim 'there is no evidence supporting it... no genome has been associated with the eukaryotic flagellar apparatus despite efforts to find one'. Also the rejection count, as 'reportedly having been rejected by more than a dozen journals'.

https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/origin-mitosing-cells-1967-lynn-sagan — Embryo Project Encyclopedia (Arizona State University), independent second source. Confirms the paper appeared in the Journal of Theoretical Biology in 1967 under the name Lynn Sagan — she had divorced Carl Sagan and kept the name, remarrying later to become Lynn Margulis — gives the citation as J. Theor. Biol. 14 (1967): 225-274, and describes the (9+2) basal bodies as sitting at the base of whip-like structures such as the sperm flagellum.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and the rejection count is deliberately vague on screen. Gray says 'reportedly... more than a dozen'; the Embryo Project says 'at least fifteen'. Those do not agree, and Gray flags his own figure as hearsay, so the beats say 'more than a dozen' and no number is set at 300px. Also not stated: the month of publication. The Embryo Project contradicts itself inside one page, saying both 'the March 1967 edition' and 'published in June 1967', so the beats say only 1967. The actual correction, and the reason this topic is worth making: the popular version is 'rejected fifteen times, then totally vindicated'. She made three claims and two of them are now textbook. The third — that the eukaryotic flagellum came from a swallowed spirochaete — has had no evidence in nearly sixty years. Do not smooth that into a triumph story. She is credited as Lynn Sagan because that is the name on the 1967 paper; the kicker does the work of connecting it.

beats.lead: There is other DNA inside you
beats.text: It is not yours.
beats.note: Your mitochondria carry their own genome. It reads as bacterial, and it says they descend from a group called the alpha-proteobacteria.

beats.name: Lynn Sagan
beats.role: She published under her married name, before she was Lynn Margulis. More than a dozen journals turned the paper down before one took it.

beats.text: Two of them are textbooks now.
beats.note: Mitochondria were bacteria. So were the chloroplasts in plants. Both were settled by reading the DNA those organelles still carry.

beats.text: Still has nothing behind it.
beats.note: She said the cell's whip-like tail came from a swallowed bacterium too. No genome has ever been found in it. It is the part nobody quotes.

beats.text: Vindicated is not the same as correct.

beats.line: The paper a dozen journals refused is now chapter one.

sources: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-56965-z — Neves, Hvidepil, Sørensen-Hygum, Stuart & Møbjerg, 'Thermotolerance experiments on active and desiccated states of Ramazzottius varieornatus emphasize that tardigrades are sensitive to high temperatures', Scientific Reports 10:94 (2020). The numbers on screen: 50% mortality at 37.1°C for non-acclimated active tardigrades, rising only to 37.6°C after acclimation; desiccated specimens at 82.7°C for 1-hour exposures, falling to 63.1°C over 24 hours.

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11084-016-9522-1 — Kaczmarek, Roszkowska et al., 'Tardigrades in Space Research – Past and Future', Origins of Life and Evolution of Biospheres (PMC5705745, PMID 27766455), full text retrieved via PubMed. Independent confirmation that active tardigrades survive only to about 38°C, that anhydrobiotic ones tolerate −272.8°C to about 150°C for 15 minutes and 5000 Gy of ionising radiation, and — the correction to the correction — that 'tardigrades in the active state are almost as resistant to radiation as in anhydrobiosis'.

https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2008.06.048 — Jönsson, Rabbow, Schill, Harms-Ringdahl & Rettberg, 'Tardigrades survive exposure to space in low Earth orbit', Current Biology 18(17):R729-R731 (2008), PMID 18786368, located via PubMed. The FOTON-M3 result behind the 'survives space' claim: they survived the vacuum, and adding solar UV and cosmic radiation significantly reduced survival.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 15 Aug 2026. This topic was nearly written wrong and the near-miss is worth recording. The draft correction was 'tardigrades are only tough when dried out' — which is false. Kaczmarek et al. state plainly that active tardigrades resist radiation almost as well as anhydrobiotic ones. Heat is the specific exception, not toughness in general, and the fourth beat now says so rather than letting the viewer over-generalise. The figure beat is 37 and it earns the 300px: the whole video is that an animal which survives vacuum and near absolute zero dies at roughly human body temperature. It is written as the integer 37 with the precise 37.1 in the context line, and that is NOT a rounding preference — FigureBeat computes its count-up with parseInt(String(value).replace(/[^0-9]/g,'')), so a value of '37.1' silently renders as a giant 371 and '1,300' as 1300. Integers only. Note 37.1 is an LT50 for one species, Ramazzottius varieornatus, so the beats say 'half a test population' and never 'they die at 37'.

beats.lead: The animal famous for surviving space
beats.text: Dies in a warm bath.
beats.note: Dried out, it handles vacuum, huge radiation doses and temperatures near absolute zero. Awake and hydrated it is a different animal.

beats.context: Where half a test population of active tardigrades died. The measured figure was 37.1. Your own body runs at 37.0.

beats.name: Neves and Møbjerg
beats.role: In Copenhagen they heated the same species in both states. Dried, half survived an hour at 82 degrees. Awake, half were dead before 38.

beats.text: Radiation barely notices whether they are awake.
beats.note: Active ones resist it almost as well as dried ones. Heat is the exception, and the one the myth leaves out.

beats.text: It is not indestructible. It is dehydrated.

beats.line: The trick is knowing when to dry out.

sources: https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2018/11/henk_rogers_on_his_first_impressions_of_tetris_and_persuading_nintendo_to_bundle_it_with_the_game_boy — Rogers' own account of the Arakawa conversation, given to IGN Japan and quoted in translation: 'If you want little boys to buy your Game Boy, pack in Mario. But if you want everyone to buy your Game Boy, pack in Tetris... And then you can still sell Mario afterwards and make more money!'

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_Game_Boy_video_games — Tetris released in Japan 14 June 1989, frequently bundled with the Game Boy, over 35 million copies shipped worldwide (citing the Telegraph, 2009); Super Mario Land over 18 million sold.

https://www.historyvshollywood.com/reelfaces/tetris-movie/ — the February 1989 Moscow negotiation with Nikolai Belikov at Elorg for the handheld rights; Rogers there on a tourist visa, quoting his own 2014 Guardian piece ('I was breaking a cardinal rule — trying to do business on a tourist visa'); the USSR, not Pajitnov, owned the rights.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. The Arakawa exchange is Rogers' own retelling, given in Japanese to IGN Japan and quoted in translation by Nintendo Life — the beat says 'as he tells it' because no second party to the conversation has ever corroborated the wording. 35 million is 'shipped', per Wikipedia's best-selling list citing the Telegraph; looser 'sold' claims circulate and are avoided. The kicker's eighteen million is Super Mario Land's own tally from the same list — it is what makes 'you can still sell Mario afterwards' a pitch that was right twice, and it is why the kicker earns its place. Deliberately not said: that Tetris 'saved' the Game Boy, any figure for what the rights cost, and anything about Pajitnov's royalties — he got nothing until 1996, which is a different video.

beats.lead: The 1989 launch bundle was almost Mario
beats.text: Tetris got the box instead.
beats.note: Nintendo of America's president saw no reason to pack in anything but his own plumber. A rival publisher talked him out of it.

beats.name: Henk Rogers
beats.role: That February he had flown to Moscow on a tourist visa and negotiated the handheld rights out of Elorg, the Soviet agency that owned Tetris. Then he went to see Arakawa about the box.

beats.lead: His pitch, as he tells it
beats.text: Mario is for little boys.
beats.note: 'If you want everyone to buy your Game Boy, pack in Tetris — young, old, male, female. And then you can still sell Mario afterwards.'

beats.context: Copies of Game Boy Tetris shipped worldwide, most of them riding in the box with the console itself.

beats.text: Mario still sold eighteen million. Afterwards.

beats.line: The right pack-in sells the machine.

sources: http://allincolorforaquarter.blogspot.com/2013/11/video-game-myth-busters-space-invaders.html — the Golden Age Arcade Historian's investigation: the shortage story traced back through UPI and the New York Times (November 1980, 'triple its production') to a September 1980 Sydney Morning Herald piece, with no earlier print source found; Paradis of the Bank of Canada's Currency Museum contacted the Bank of Japan (no evidence of a shortage found) and the Japan Mint (production increase 'had nothing to do with Space Invaders'), and cites Nishikado calling the story a wild rumour.

https://www.academia.edu/2568838/Space_Invaders_targets_coins — Mark Fox, World Coin News, February 2012, the origin of the production table (from the 1995 Krause guide): 440 million 100-yen coins struck in 1977, 292 million in 1978, 382 million in 1979, 588 million in 1980. Figures read as reproduced in full in the blog post above.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Invaders — Japan release July 1978, Tomohiro Nishikado sole designer, who also engineered its custom hardware; the speed-up: the processor rendered frames faster as aliens were destroyed, so the survivors accelerated, and Nishikado kept the undocumented behaviour as the game's difficulty mechanism.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. NO figure beat: the mint numbers only mean anything as a pair — 440 million falling to 292 million — and a lone giant number would assert nothing. Release month is deliberately absent: Wikipedia says July 1978, the numismatic sources say June, so the beats say only the year. Cabinet sales are absent for the same reason (55,000-65,000 US and 200,000-400,000 worldwide ranges do not reconcile). The beats never affirm 'the mint tripled production' even to deny it precisely; what the record supports is that production FELL in the release year, no shortage was ever documented by the Bank of Japan, and the story cannot be traced earlier than September 1980 — more than two years after release. The speed-up accident is the well-documented counterweight: the famous thing about the game that IS true. Nishikado's 'wild rumour' line is secondhand (the Mint's PR office citing an interview, via Paradis, via the blog), so the kicker says 'calls it a rumour' and no more.

beats.text: Japan never ran out of coins.
beats.note: Space Invaders was said to have drained the nation's 100-yen supply until the mint tripled production. The claim has been in print since 1980. Nobody checked it for thirty years.

beats.name: Tomohiro Nishikado
beats.role: He designed Space Invaders at Taito and engineered its hardware himself. The craze was real — the coin story grew on top of it, surfacing in foreign papers two years later.

beats.text: Production fell the year it launched.
beats.note: Japan struck 440 million 100-yen coins in 1977 and 292 million in 1978. The Bank of Japan, asked directly, could find no record of a shortage at all.

beats.text: The speed-up was a bug.
beats.note: Fewer aliens meant the processor drew frames faster, so the survivors accelerated. Nishikado kept it — and the arcade difficulty curve was born as a hardware limit.

beats.text: Even Nishikado calls the coin story a rumour.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthill_report — commissioned by the Science Research Council in 1972, published 1973 in 'Artificial Intelligence: a paper symposium'; the verdict quoted verbatim: 'In no part of the field have the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised'; it 'formed the basis for the decision by the British government to end support for AI research in most British universities' (Russell & Norvig); the 9 May 1973 Royal Institution debate against Michie, McCarthy and Gregory; the combinatorial-explosion argument.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_winter — the debate was broadcast in the BBC 'Controversy' series under the title 'The general purpose robot is a mirage'; UK AI research continued at only Edinburgh, Essex and Sussex; large-scale funding returned only with Alvey's £350 million in 1983; the term 'AI winter' first appeared at the 1984 AAAI meeting, where Schank and Minsky — by analogy with nuclear winter — warned the business community the 1980s boom would collapse, and 'three years later the billion-dollar AI industry began to collapse.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. NO figure beat. Candidates were 25 (the report's own forecast horizon — a prediction, not a fact), £350 million (Alvey's 1983 war chest — carried in the sign, where it reads as a bill rather than a headline), and 1984 (a date). None deserves 300px. The two Wikipedia pages disagree on who asked for the report — the AI-winter page says the UK Parliament, the Lighthill-report page says the Science Research Council commissioned it in 1972 — and the beats follow the SRC version, which matches the report's own publication. Deliberately not said: that Lighthill caused the American winter (DARPA's 1973-74 cuts had their own politics), any claim about who won the televised debate (no source scores it), and 'ended ALL British AI research' — Edinburgh, Essex and Sussex kept going, and the credit beat says so.

beats.lead: AI's first collapse had an author
beats.text: One report froze the field.
beats.note: In 1972 Britain's Science Research Council asked an outsider to survey artificial intelligence. He was a fluid dynamicist, not a computer scientist.

beats.name: James Lighthill
beats.role: His survey concluded that in no part of the field had the discoveries produced 'the major impact that was then promised.' British funding collapsed; the work survived at just Edinburgh, Essex and Sussex.

beats.text: The general purpose robot is a mirage.
beats.note: The BBC staged the debate under that title in its Controversy series: Lighthill versus McCarthy, Michie and Gregory at the Royal Institution, May 1973. The recording still circulates.

beats.lead: The name arrived a decade late
beats.text: AI winter, after nuclear winter.
beats.note: Coined at a 1984 AAAI debate, where Schank and Minsky warned the new boom would collapse the same way. Three years later the billion-dollar AI industry did.

beats.text: The second winter arrived on schedule.

beats.line: Britain paid £350 million to restart what one report stopped.

sources: https://invention.si.edu/invention-stories/mother-all-demos — Smithsonian Lemelson Center, deeply footnoted: the 9 December 1968 90-minute plenary at the ACM/IEEE Fall Joint Computer Conference, San Francisco; the NLS 30 miles away in Menlo Park, reached over a homemade 2,400-baud modem on a leased phone line with video returned by microwave link; the first mouse invented by Engelbart and BUILT by Bill English in 1964 — wooden shell, two perpendicular wheels, one button; 'no one could remember exactly who first coined the term... it just looked like a mouse with a tail'; Engelbart's recollection of the audience 'standing, cheering like crazy'; the phrase 'mother of all demos' first used by Steven Levy in Insanely Great (1994), p. 42.

https://cybercultural.com/p/1968-the-mother-of-all-demos/ — Richard MacManus's account, corroborating the date, the ~30-mile Menlo Park link, the wooden mouse with the cord 'like a tail on a mouse', the chord keyset, the on-screen collaboration with Bill Paxton, and Engelbart's own on-stage words: 'I don't know why we call it a mouse... it started that way and we never did change it.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. The figure beat is 30 and it earns the 300px: the demo's whole trick was that the machine was not in the room — live interactive computing carried thirty miles in 1968 — and both sources give the distance. Candidates cut: 90 (minutes — a duration), 2400 (baud — jargon at that size; it lives in the context line), and the audience count (Smithsonian implies the 2,000-seat Brooks Hall, cybercultural says 'hundreds'; they do not agree, so no number appears). The ovation is Engelbart's own recollection from a Wired interview, and the kicker words it as his memory. Deliberately not said: 'Engelbart invented the mouse' unqualified — English built it, and the credit is shared in the beat; also the entire patent-and-royalties saga (the $40,000 Apple licence figure is single-sourced folklore) and any straight line from the demo to the Macintosh.

beats.text: It was all demoed at once.
beats.note: The mouse, windows, hypertext, video calls, live shared editing — shown working together in San Francisco in 1968, before any of it was a product.

beats.name: Douglas Engelbart
beats.role: 9 December, a 90-minute session at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. He sat alone on stage under the lights, driving a computer the audience could not see.

beats.context: The computer was in Menlo Park, that far away. A homemade 2,400-baud modem carried his keystrokes; microwave dishes beamed the video back.

beats.lead: The pointer already had its name
beats.text: The cord looked like a tail.
beats.note: Bill English built the first mouse in 1964 from Engelbart's sketches: a wooden shell, two metal wheels, one button. On stage, Engelbart admitted nobody remembered who named it.

beats.text: He remembered the crowd standing, cheering like crazy.

beats.line: Steven Levy later gave it a title: the mother of all demos.

sources: https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/51674/history-ctrl-alt-delete — the full Bradley account: spring 1981, Boca Raton, the rushed one-year Acorn project; reboots triggering slow memory tests ('Some days, you'd be rebooting every five minutes'); 'it was five minutes, 10 minutes of activity, and then I moved on'; keys chosen by position so all three could not be pressed accidentally; never intended for customers; the 2001 20th-anniversary panel; and the 2013 framing that Gates admitted the login use was a mistake and blamed IBM.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bradley_(engineer) — one of the twelve engineers on the original IBM PC, author of its ROM BIOS; the combination meant for developers and technical writers, not end users; keys chosen (with Mel Hallerman) as practically impossible to press by accident; revealed to the public through IBM's own technical reference documentation; the verbatim quote at The Tech Museum, 8 August 2001, on a panel with Gates: 'I have to share the credit. I may have invented it, but I think Bill made it famous.'
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. NO figure beat. Candidates: 12 (his place on the team — an ordinal), 5 (minutes — a duration, the same trap the standard records for the moth relay), and 500 million (PCs sold by 2001 — true but belongs to a different story). Wikipedia names Mel Hallerman as co-chooser of the keys, so the beat says the keys 'were chosen' rather than crediting Bradley alone. The kicker drops the quote's lead-in ('I have to share the credit') for length — the same edit every press account makes, flagged here so nobody restores it into a beat that cannot hold it. Multiple-key reboots predate IBM (Exidy Sorcerer, 1978), so the beats never say Bradley invented the concept — 'invented' appears only inside his own quoted joke. The Gates 'mistake' line is asserted by Mental Floss directly; the Verge piece it cites was not reachable from here, so the sign claims no more than Mental Floss itself does.

beats.lead: It was never meant for you
beats.text: It was a private developer tool.
beats.note: Rebooting IBM's prototype PC meant sitting through memory tests on every restart. The team hunting bugs rebooted every five minutes. One of them got tired of waiting.

beats.name: David Bradley
beats.role: The 12th of 12 engineers on the secret PC project in Boca Raton. His instant-reboot shortcut took five or ten minutes, one item on a list of a hundred tasks.

beats.text: One hand cannot press them.
beats.note: Del sat across the keyboard from Ctrl and Alt, so no accident could trigger it. The public only found out because IBM printed it in the technical manual.

beats.text: I may have invented it, but Bill made it famous.

beats.line: In 2013, Gates agreed it was a mistake.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Room_coffee_pot — the 1991 setup by Quentin Stafford-Fraser (client, XCoffee) and Paul Jardetzky (server) at Cambridge's Computer Laboratory; 128×128 greyscale camera on an Acorn Archimedes capture card; the purpose (sparing researchers the trip to an empty pot); November 1993, Daniel Gordon and Martyn Johnson put the feed on the web once browsers could show images; switched off 09:54 UTC, 22 August 2001, with front-page coverage in The Times and The Washington Post; the final Krups auctioned on eBay for £3,350 to Der Spiegel, later refurbished pro bono by Krups.

https://quentinsf.com/coffeepot/ — Stafford-Fraser's own page: he disclaims sole invention ('I certainly didn't do it single-handed'); first press was Bob Metcalfe's 1992 Communications Week column, when it was a networked camera but not yet a webcam; since 2016 the pot sits in the Heinz Nixdorf MuseumsForum in Paderborn with, in his words, a webcam pointing at it.
topics.verifiedNote: Checked 17 Aug 2026. NO figure beat, and £3,350 deliberately stays at note size: FigureBeat leaves roughly 550px of unit space beside a TWO-digit value, so a four-digit 3350 would squeeze 'pounds' into the same clipped-edge failure the _README records for 'photoreceptors'. Other candidates cut: 128 (pixels — a spec, not a fact that carries the story) and 10 (years — a duration). No frame rate is claimed anywhere because neither source commits to one. The often-quoted 2.4 million visitors appears in neither source read here and is left out. The credit beat names both builders because Stafford-Fraser himself corrects the 'lone inventor' framing. The kicker — a webcam now pointed at the retired pot in the Paderborn museum — is from his page, where the live image is embedded.

beats.lead: The first webcam had one job
beats.text: Is there coffee, or not.
beats.note: Cambridge's Computer Laboratory had seven floors and one filter machine. In 1991, researchers pointed a camera at it so nobody climbed the stairs to an empty pot.

beats.name: Stafford-Fraser and Jardetzky
beats.role: One wrote the client — XCoffee — and the other the server, feeding a 128-by-128 greyscale image of the pot to every desk on the lab network.

beats.text: The pot joined the web.
beats.note: Browsers had just learned to display images. Daniel Gordon and Martyn Johnson put the feed on a page, and the lab's coffee became visible worldwide.

beats.text: They switched it off.
beats.note: The shutdown made the front pages of The Times and The Washington Post. The last pot went to eBay, where Der Spiegel paid £3,350 for it.

beats.text: A webcam now points at it, in a museum.

beats.line: Ten years pointed at a coffee pot.
